mainTopic: Changed stolen items and תקנת השבים: when a robber may pay money instead, and the decree not to accept repayment from repentant robbers and lenders who took interest.
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier discussion: some said the הלכה follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, though שמואל himself does not hold that way. Next, רבי יוחנן teaches that by Torah law a stolen item that has changed still goes back as is. Our משנה lets the robber pay money instead only because of תקנת השבים, a rabbinic rule that makes repentance easier. רבי יעקב explains that רבי יוחנן meant only a change that can be undone, so his view fits the משנה about dyed wool. The גמרא then teaches a further decree from the days of רבי: we do not accept repayment from robbers or lenders who took interest. That decree was made after a man gave up on תשובה when his wife told him even his belt was stolen. The גמרא defends this decree against several ברייתות that seem to require repayment. Its answers include children returning a recognizable item to honor a father who repented, offers made only 'to fulfill their duty to Heaven,' and sources dated to before the decree. At the end, רב נחמן's rule that the decree applies only when the stolen item is gone opens a new way to reconcile the sources, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Closing note: the ruling follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, but שמואל himself disagrees
steps.stepSummary: An alternate report says the הלכה is like רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, though שמואל personally does not hold that way.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some said that the הלכה is like רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. But he himself does not agree with that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an earlier discussion. Some reported that the הלכה follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, and the גמרא adds that שמואל himself does not hold that way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a report of what others said, not a new argument. The point is that a ruling can be passed along in a person's name even when that person does not personally agree with it. Once this is said, the earlier discussion is closed and the גמרא moves to a new topic.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical ruling we follow
He does not hold that way

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר.
phrases.english: Some said: the halacha is like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
But he himself does not hold that way.
phrases.notes: "He himself" is שמואל, whose view the גמרא was talking about just before this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion from the previous section of the daf.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Others reported that the הלכה is like רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, but שמואל does not personally hold that way.

steps.title: By Torah law, a changed stolen item is returned as is
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that by Torah law, a robber must return the stolen item itself even after it has changed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: By Torah law, a stolen item that has changed goes back as it is. The פסוק says "he shall return the stolen item that he stole," which means in every case.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבי יוחנן says that by Torah law, a change to a stolen item does not let the robber keep it, so he must give back the item itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source is the פסוק "והשיב את הגזלה אשר גזל." It says to return "the stolen item" with no limits, so it applies even when the item has changed. On the Torah level, then, a change does not transfer ownership to the robber.

keyTerms.meaning: By Torah law, as opposed to a rabbinic rule
A stolen item that has been changed
Is returned as it is, the item itself
In any case, no matter what

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main tension of the סוגיא: if the Torah says the item goes back, why does our משנה let the robber pay money instead?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
By Torah law,
a stolen item that has changed is returned as it is.
As it says: "And he shall return the stolen item that he stole"
meaning, in every case.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new discussion about whether a change lets the robber keep the stolen item.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By Torah law, a change does not let the robber keep the item, so the item itself must be returned.

steps.title: Our משנה lets the robber pay only because of תקנת השבים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers in advance the objection from our משנה: its rule that the robber pays money is a rabbinic rule made to help robbers repent.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will ask from our משנה, which says the robber pays money instead of returning the changed item: that rule is only because of the enactment made for people who repent.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן raises a question against himself and answers it right away. Our משנה lets the robber keep a changed item and pay money, and he says that is only a rabbinic rule to encourage robbers to repent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The objection is that our משנה seems to say a change does transfer the item to the robber. The answer is that the Torah law has not changed. The חכמים added a rule so that a robber who wants to repent is not stuck having to return a reworked item.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say; this introduces an expected objection
Our משנה, the one in this perek
The enactment made for people who repent

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי יוחנן is saying the משנה is wrong. He agrees with its rule in practice. He is only saying that the reason for it is rabbinic, not Torah law.

phrases.english: And if you will say: but our mishna rules otherwise!
phrases.notes: Our משנה says a robber who changed the item pays what it was worth when he stole it, instead of returning it.

phrases.english: That is because of the enactment for those who repent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבי יוחנן's Torah rule against an obvious objection from our משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains that the משנה's rule is rabbinic, not Torah law.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Our משנה seems to show that a change makes the item belong to the robber even by Torah law.
steps.terutzMaskana: By Torah law the item goes back. The robber pays money instead only because of תקנת השבים.

steps.title: Challenge: רבי יוחנן also rules like an unattributed משנה that treats dyeing as a real change
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי יוחנן could say this. He also rules that the הלכה follows an unattributed משנה, and such a משנה treats dyed wool as changed enough to cancel the obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי יוחנן really say that? But רבי יוחנן said the הלכה follows an unattributed משנה, and a משנה teaches: if he did not manage to give the wool to the כהן before he dyed it, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן with another one of his own rules. He holds that we follow an unattributed משנה, and that kind of משנה shows that a change such as dyeing does count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The unattributed משנה about ראשית הגז says that dyeing the wool exempts the owner from giving it to the כהן, so a change cancels the obligation by Torah law. If רבי יוחנן follows that משנה, how can he say a change never counts by Torah law in robbery? His two statements seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Did he really say this?
An unattributed משנה, one stated without naming a תנא
Exempt

phrases.english: But did Rabbi Yochanan really say this?!

phrases.aramaic: וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הֲלָכָה כִּסְתַם מִשְׁנָה,
phrases.english: But Rabbi Yochanan said: the halacha follows an unattributed mishna,
and we learned: if he did not manage to give it to him
phrases.notes: This משנה is in חולין and is about ראשית הגז, the first shearing that goes to the כהן. "Him" is the כהן.

phrases.english: before he dyed it, he is exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the Torah rule from step 2 using another statement of רבי יוחנן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's claim that by Torah law a changed stolen item is returned as is.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן follows an unattributed משנה, and such a משנה treats dyeing as a change that cancels an obligation. That contradicts his claim that a change does not count by Torah law.

steps.title: רבי יעקב: רבי יוחנן meant a change that can be undone
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב reports that רבי יוחנן explained his rule to him: it applies to sanded wood made into vessels, a change that can return to its original state.
steps.simpleTranslation: One of the חכמים, named רבי יעקב, said to them: רבי יוחנן explained it to me himself. He meant a case where someone stole sanded boards and made them into vessels. That is a change that can go back to how it was.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יעקב answers the contradiction. He says רבי יוחנן's rule covers only a change that can be undone, so it does not clash with the dyed-wool משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vessels made from sanded boards can be taken apart and turned back into boards, so the change is not permanent. A change like that does not count by Torah law, and the item goes back. Dyeing wool is a permanent change, so it does count, and the two rulings fit together.

keyTerms.meaning: It was explained to me personally
Sanded or smoothed boards
A change that can return to its original state
For example; such as the case of

steps.whatToRemember: By Torah law, a change that can be undone does not let the robber keep the item, and it goes back as is. When our משנה lets him pay money instead in such a case, that is only because of תקנת השבים. A permanent change, like dyeing, already counts by Torah law.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up a key distinction for the whole topic: a change that can be undone versus a permanent one.

phrases.english: One of the Rabbis said to them,
and his name was Rabbi Yaakov:

phrases.aramaic: לְדִידִי מִפָּרְשָׁא לִי מִינֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן –
phrases.english: It was explained to me by Rabbi Yochanan himself:
For example, where he stole sanded boards
and made them into vessels,
which is a change that can go back to its original state.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ הַהוּא מִדְּרַבָּנַן וְרַבִּי יַעֲקֹב שְׁמֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 4 by narrowing the case of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the case: רבי יוחנן's rule covers only a change that can be undone.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן said every change leaves the item returnable by Torah law, which contradicts the dyed-wool משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: His rule covers only a change that can be undone, like boards made into vessels. A permanent change like dyeing does count by Torah law.

steps.title: Do not accept repayment from robbers or lenders who charged interest
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that when robbers or lenders who took רבית try to return what they took, the victim should not accept it. The חכמים are unhappy with anyone who does accept it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If robbers or people who lent money for interest come to give back what they took, we do not accept it from them. Whoever does accept it from them, the Sages are not pleased with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with another rabbinic rule designed to make תשובה easier for robbers and lenders who took interest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes even further than the rule in Step 3, where the robber may pay money instead of returning the changed item. Here the victim is told not to take back the stolen goods or the interest at all. Accepting is not forbidden outright, but the חכמים frown on it because it discourages sinners from repenting.

keyTerms.meaning: Robbers, people who take things openly by force
People who lend money and charge interest, which the Torah forbids
The Sages are not pleased with him. This is disapproval, not a formal prohibition.

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how far the חכמים went to keep the door to תשובה open, even giving up a victim's rightful claim.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Robbers and those who lend with interest who returned [what they took]
one does not accept it from them.
And one who accepts from them
the spirit of the Sages is not pleased with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַגַּזְלָנִין וּמַלְוֵי בְּרִבִּית שֶׁהֶחְזִירוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the dyed-wool discussion to another rabbinic rule made to help sinners do תשובה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Victims should not accept repayment from repentant robbers or lenders who charged interest. The חכמים disapprove of anyone who does.

steps.title: The story behind the decree in the days of רבי
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the decree was made in the days of רבי. A man wanted to do תשובה, but his wife mocked him that even his belt was stolen, so he gave up. The חכמים then made the decree.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: This teaching was made in the days of רבי. As a ברייתא teaches: A man once wanted to repent. His wife said to him: 'Empty one! If you repent, even your belt isn't yours!' So he held back and did not repent. At that time the Sages said: If robbers or lenders with interest come to give back what they took, we do not accept it. Whoever does accept it, the Sages are not pleased with him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן tells us when and why the decree from Step 6 was made, and supports it with a story from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story shows the exact problem the decree solves. When everything a sinner owns has to be returned, the cost can make him give up on תשובה completely. Taking away the duty to repay removed that obstacle.

keyTerms.meaning: In the days of רבי יהודה הנשיא
Was taught or established
Empty one, a word of insult
Belt or sash
Repentance, returning to proper behavior

steps.whyThisMatters: It gives the reason behind the decree. That reason matters in Step 8, where the גמרא tests how far the decree reaches.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: בִּימֵי רַבִּי נִשְׁנֵית מִשְׁנָה זוֹ.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said: This teaching was taught in the days of Rabbi.
phrases.notes: 'This משנה' means the ברייתא we just learned in Step 6, not a משנה in our פרק.

phrases.english: As it is taught: There was an incident with one man
who wanted to repent.
His wife said to him: Empty one!
If you repent,
even the belt is not yours!
And he held back and did not repent.
At that time they said:
Robbers and those who lend with interest who returned [what they took]
one does not accept it from them,
and one who accepts from them
the spirit of the Sages is not pleased with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: בִּימֵי רַבִּי נִשְׁנֵית מִשְׁנָה זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the historical background and reason for the decree in Step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The decree was made in רבי's time because the burden of full repayment was stopping sinners from doing תשובה.

steps.title: Challenge: a father who took interest seems obligated to return it
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says children who inherit interest money do not have to return it. The גמרא infers that their father did have to return it, which seems to clash with the decree.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: If a father left his children money that came from interest, they do not have to return it, even though they know it is interest. So the children do not have to, but their father did have to return it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the decree using a precise reading of another ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא only frees the children, which suggests the father himself was obligated. If the father had to repay, the victim may accept from him. That contradicts the decree that we do not accept repayment from a lender who took interest.

keyTerms.meaning: Money that was collected as interest
It is they who are not obligated, an inference drawn from exact wording

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא never says the father must pay. The challenge comes from what it leaves unsaid, since it only mentions the children.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:

phrases.aramaic: הִנִּיחַ לָהֶם אֲבִיהֶם מָעוֹת שֶׁל רִבִּית,
phrases.english: If their father left them money of interest,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהֵן יוֹדְעִין שֶׁהֵן רִבִּית –
phrases.english: even though they know that it is interest,
they are not obligated to return it.
It is they who are not [obligated],
but their father is obligated to return it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: הִנִּיחַ לָהֶם אֲבִיהֶם מָעוֹת שֶׁל רִבִּית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the decree of Steps 6 and 7 from a different ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The decree that we do not accept repayment from lenders who took interest.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא frees only the children, which implies the father was obligated to repay. If he was obligated, his victims could accept from him.

steps.title: The father is also exempt; the children are mentioned because of the next clause
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the father really is exempt too. The ברייתא spoke about the children only because its next clause, which requires returning a specific item out of respect for the father, can only be about them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the father also does not have to return it. The reason the ברייתא speaks about the children is that it wants to teach the next clause: 'If their father left them a cow, a garment, or any recognizable item, they must return it out of respect for their father.' So it taught the first clause about the children too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא removes the challenge by showing that the inference from the wording is not a real inference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second clause only makes sense about children, since 'respect for their father' does not apply to the father himself. To keep both clauses parallel, the ברייתא wrote the first clause about the children too. So nothing can be learned about the father from it, and the decree stands.

keyTerms.meaning: By right, really, the law is actually that
The first clause and the latter clause of a teaching
A specific, recognizable item that people know about
The honor of their father

steps.whatToRemember: Repentant lenders who took interest, and the robbers grouped with them, are not required to repay, and victims should not accept repayment. Heirs who hold a recognizable item from their father must still return it out of respect for him.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a common גמרא tool. A ברייתא's choice of wording can be explained by its later clause, which cancels an inference from the earlier one.

phrases.aramaic: בְּדִין הוּא דַּאֲבִיהֶם נָמֵי אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב לְהַחְזִיר;
phrases.english: By right, their father also is not obligated to return it;
and the reason it teaches about them
is because it wants to teach the latter clause:
'If their father left them a cow or a garment
or any recognizable item,
they are obligated to return it because of the honor of their father,'
[so] it taught the first clause also about them.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּדִין הוּא דַּאֲבִיהֶם נָמֵי אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב לְהַחְזִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 8 by rejecting the inference about the father.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the ברייתא's wording as matching its latter clause, so no inference about the father can be drawn.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the ברייתא mentions only the children, the father must have been obligated to repay.
steps.terutzMaskana: The father is also exempt. The children are mentioned only to keep the first clause parallel to the latter clause about honoring the father.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The decree stands: no one has to repay interest after doing תשובה, but heirs must return recognizable items out of respect for their father.

steps.title: Why should children honor a father who took interest?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea from step 9 that children must return a specific item out of כבוד אב. A father who took רבית is not acting like a proper Jew, so the מצוה to honor him should not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are the children really obligated to return it because of their father's honor? I can read here the פסוק: 'And a ruler among your people you shall not curse.' That means only someone who acts the way your people should act. A father who took interest does not act that way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the second clause of the ברייתא from step 9, which made the children return a specific item out of respect for their father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about not cursing a נשיא is read to protect only a ruler who behaves properly, 'בעושה מעשה עמך'. The same limit should apply to כבוד אב. A father who took רבית is a sinner, so why should his children have to protect his honor?

keyTerms.meaning: The מצוה of honoring one's father
I will read here (a פסוק that seems to contradict this)
A ruler or leader
Only one who acts like a proper member of your people

phrases.english: And because of the honor of their father
they are obligated to return it?
I will read here:
'And a ruler among your people you shall not curse'
which means only one who acts the way your people act?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning (כבוד אב) used in the ברייתא cited in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that children must return a specific item out of respect for their father.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Honor is only owed to one who acts properly; a father who took רבית does not, so there should be no obligation of honor.

steps.title: The father did תשובה
steps.stepSummary: Using רב פנחס's answer from elsewhere, the גמרא explains that the father had done תשובה, so he deserves honor again.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like רב פנחס said: the case is where he did תשובה. Here too, the case is where the father did תשובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by saying the father repented, so he is no longer a sinner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge only works if the father is still wicked. Once he has done תשובה, he again 'acts like your people', and the מצוה of כבוד אב fully applies.

keyTerms.meaning: Repentance
Here too

phrases.english: Like Rav Pinchas said:
it is where he repented;
here too, it is where he repented.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 10.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The father is a sinner who does not deserve honor.
steps.terutzMaskana: The father repented, so he deserves honor.

steps.title: If he repented, why didn't he give it back?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a father who truly repented would still have the item. Real תשובה means returning it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he did תשובה, what is the item still doing with him? He should have returned it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer of step 11. If the father really repented, he should already have returned the item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Real תשובה for taking money includes giving it back. If the item is still in the estate, that suggests the father did not truly repent.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it doing with him?
To return

phrases.english: If he repented,
what is it doing with him?
phrases.notes: Literally 'what does it want by him', meaning why is the item still in his hands?

phrases.english: He should have returned it!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה, מַאי בָּעֵי גַּבֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case setup offered in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the father did תשובה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone who truly repented would already have returned the stolen item.

steps.title: He died before he could return it
steps.stepSummary: The father repented but died before he managed to return the item, so the children return it for his honor.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where he did not manage to return it before he died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the father really repented, but he ran out of time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This keeps the father's תשובה real and keeps the item in the estate. The children return it to protect the honor of a father who wanted to fix his wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Did not manage in time

steps.whatToRemember: Children must return a specific item their father took out of כבוד אב only when the father repented but died before he could return it.

phrases.english: It is where he did not manage to return it
before he died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 12.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Real תשובה would have meant returning it already.
steps.terutzMaskana: He repented sincerely but died first.

steps.title: A ברייתא says robbers and lenders return what they took
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא seems to say that robbers and lenders with interest must return what they collected. That seems to clash with the decree not to accept it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: robbers and those who lend with interest, even though they collected it, return it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source that seems to contradict the decree from steps 6-7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The decree said victims should not accept returned goods or interest. This ברייתא says the takers 'return' it, which sounds like the money really goes back.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who lend with interest
That they collected

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Robbers and those who lend with interest,
even though they collected,
they return it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new challenge to the decree after the previous one was resolved.
steps.kashyaTarget: The decree that we do not accept back stolen goods or interest.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says they return it, which implies the return is accepted.

steps.title: What does 'collected' mean for robbers?
steps.stepSummary: Before dealing with the contradiction, the גמרא asks how the word 'collected' fits robbers. A robber simply grabs; he does not collect.
steps.simpleTranslation: Robbers — what 'collecting' is there? If they robbed, they robbed, and if they did not rob, they did not rob!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to question the wording of the ברייתא. This sets up a fixed reading in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Collecting' fits someone who takes payment based on a deal, like a lender. A robber either took by force or did not, so the word doesn't fit him.

keyTerms.meaning: Robbers
If they robbed, they robbed

phrases.english: Robbers — what 'collected' is there?
If they robbed, they robbed,
and if they did not rob, they did not rob!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Interrupts the challenge to clarify the ברייתא's wording.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the word 'collected' can apply to robbers.

steps.title: The 'robbers' are the interest lenders
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא: 'robbers' refers to lenders with interest. Then it restates the challenge: they must return what they collected.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: the robbers — and who are they? Lenders with interest. Even though they collected it, they return it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the reading so that 'robbers' describes the interest lenders, and then repeats the contradiction with the decree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now 'collected' makes sense, because lenders collect interest through their deal. The ברייתא calls them robbers, and it still says they return the money. That clashes with the decree.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say (read the text this way)
And who are they?

phrases.english: Rather, say: the robbers,
and who are they? Lenders with interest;
even though they collected it, they return it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question of step 15 and restates the challenge of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Robbers' is a description of interest lenders, so 'collected' fits.

steps.title: They give it back, but it is not accepted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the ברייתא means the lenders offer to return the interest, but the victim does not accept it. This fits the decree.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: they return it, but we do not accept it from them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by reading 'they return' as only the lender's side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא describes the lender's duty to offer the money back. The decree tells the victim not to take it. Both rules hold together.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not accept it from them

steps.whatToRemember: Even after the decree, a lender with interest still offers to return it. The decree only tells the victim not to accept it.
steps.confusionAlert: 'מחזירין' here does not mean the money actually changes hands. It means the lender offers it, and the victim refuses.

phrases.english: They say:
they return it, but we do not accept it from them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in steps 14 and 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the source to fit both rules
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'They return' means the victim takes the money back, which goes against the decree.
steps.terutzMaskana: The lender offers it back, but the victim does not accept it.

steps.title: Why offer it back if no one will take it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the point is of the lenders offering back the interest, if the victim will refuse it anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if it won't be accepted, why do they offer it back at all?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer it just gave in step 17. This sets up the next line, which explains the purpose of the offer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 17 said the lenders offer the interest back, but the victim does not accept it. That sounds like a pointless gesture. So the גמרא asks what the offer actually accomplishes.

keyTerms.meaning: They return / give back
But / if so (here: 'but then')

phrases.english: But why do they return it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the purpose of the answer given in step 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the purpose is of offering back money that will not be accepted.

steps.title: To fulfill their duty to Heaven
steps.stepSummary: They offer it back so that their repentance is complete before Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: To fulfill their obligation to Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the offer is how the sinner fulfills his duty to Heaven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The victim may refuse because of the decree. Still, the sinner must show he truly wants to fix his wrong. The sincere offer is part of a full תשובה.

keyTerms.meaning: To fulfill one's obligation toward Heaven

phrases.english: To fulfill their obligation to Heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The offer is made to fulfill their duty to Heaven, even though the victim refuses it.

steps.title: A ברייתא says shepherds and tax collectors must return what they took
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא says shepherds, tax collectors and customs collectors must return what they took to the people they recognize. That seems to clash with the decree not to accept it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: for shepherds, tax collectors and customs collectors, repentance is hard, and they must return what they took to the people they recognize!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא as a challenge. It says these kinds of thieves really do return what they stole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The decree says we do not accept stolen money back from a repentant robber. This ברייתא says these robbers give it back to every victim they can identify. That looks like a contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: Shepherds (who let their flocks graze in other people's fields)
Tax collectors and customs collectors
People they recognize (as their victims)

phrases.english: Come and hear: shepherds, tax collectors, and customs collectors:
their repentance is hard, and they return to those they recognize!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a new contradiction from a different ברייתא, similar to step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The decree not to accept stolen money back from a repentant robber.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says these robbers return what they took to known victims. That implies the victims accept it.

steps.title: They offer it, but no one accepts it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries the same answer as before: the robbers offer it back, but the victims do not accept it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: they offer it back, but we don't accept it from them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge the same way it answered step 14. The ברייתא only means the robbers offer it back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This reads 'they return' as 'they offer to return.' The ruling of the decree stays in place, because the victim still refuses.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not accept it from them

phrases.english: They say: they return it, but one does not accept it from them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 using the same idea as step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא means the robbers actually pay back their victims.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only means they offer to pay, and the victims refuse.

steps.title: Again: why offer it back?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא again asks what the point of offering is, if no one accepts.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then why do they offer it back?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the same question it asked in step 18, now about this ברייתא. It is setting up the same answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא really does repeat these words. It is running the same reasoning on the new ברייתא, to show the full answer before testing it.

keyTerms.meaning: And but then

phrases.english: But then why do they return it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the purpose of the answer in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why offer what will not be accepted.

steps.title: Again: to fulfill their duty to Heaven
steps.stepSummary: The same answer: the offer fulfills their duty to Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: To fulfill their obligation to Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same answer as in step 19.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the full answer is in place: the offer is made for Heaven's sake, and no money changes hands. The next step will test this answer.

phrases.english: To fulfill their obligation to Heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The offer is made to fulfill their duty to Heaven.

steps.title: Then why is their repentance hard?
steps.stepSummary: If they never really have to pay anything back, why does the ברייתא call their repentance hard?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why is their repentance hard?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave. The ברייתא's words 'their repentance is hard' don't fit it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Repentance is hard because they must track down many victims and pay each one. If they only make an offer that gets refused, nothing is hard about it. So the ברייתא must mean they really pay.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Why?
Their repentance is difficult

phrases.english: If so, why is their repentance hard?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of steps 21 and 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that they only offer and the victims do not accept.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא calls their repentance hard, which only makes sense if they must actually pay.

steps.title: The end of the ברייתא proves money is really paid
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's last part says money for unknown victims goes to public needs, and רב חסדא says that means pits, ditches and caves. So money really leaves the robber's hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: And also, read the end: for victims they don't recognize, they should use the money for public needs. And רב חסדא said: pits, ditches and caves!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second challenge from the end of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If money must be spent on public projects, then it really is given away, not just offered. This can't be explained as an offer that gets refused.

keyTerms.meaning: And furthermore (adds a second challenge)
The latter clause of a source
Public needs
Pits, ditches and caves (water storage for public use)

phrases.english: And furthermore, say the latter clause:

phrases.aramaic: וְשֶׁאֵין מַכִּירִין – יַעֲשֶׂה בָּהֶן צׇרְכֵי צִיבּוּר,
phrases.english: and for those they do not recognize, he should use it for public needs,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: בּוֹרוֹת, שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת!
phrases.english: and Rav Ḥisda said: pits, ditches and caves!
phrases.notes: These are water pits and cisterns everyone can use, so the stolen money benefits the public, including the victims.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, stronger challenge to the answer of step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that they only offer and the victims do not accept.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Spending the money on public projects shows it is really paid out, not refused.

steps.title: Before the decree versus after the decree
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops its earlier answer. This ברייתא is from before the decree, when robbers really paid back. The other source is from after the decree, when it is not accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, there is no difficulty: here it is before the decree, there it is after the decree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up the 'offer but no acceptance' answer. It solves the contradiction by time: before the decree and after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אֶלָּא shows the old answer is dropped. The ברייתא about shepherds and collectors comes from before the decree, so they really paid. After the decree was made, the money is not accepted from a robber who repents.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult (no contradiction)
Here... there (splitting two sources into two cases)
Rabbinic decree (here: not to accept stolen money back from repentant robbers)

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא that says robbers must pay back comes from before the decree. After the decree, we do not accept stolen money back from a robber who repents. The 'they only offer it' answer was dropped for this ברייתא.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the 'offer but don't accept' answer is still standing here. The word אֶלָּא tells you the גמרא abandoned it for this ברייתא and switched to a time-based answer.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a ruling can change over time because of a rabbinic decree. A source from before the decree should not be read as arguing with the law after it.

phrases.english: Rather, it is not difficult:

phrases.aramaic: כָּאן קוֹדֶם תַּקָּנָה, כָּאן לְאַחַר תַּקָּנָה.
phrases.english: here it is before the decree, there it is after the decree.
phrases.notes: The decree is the one not to accept stolen money back from robbers who repent, which the סוגיא has been discussing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָא קַשְׁיָא; כָּאן קוֹדֶם תַּקָּנָה, כָּאן לְאַחַר תַּקָּנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Abandons the answer that failed in steps 24 and 25, and gives a new resolution to the contradiction of step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the sources by time (before and after the decree)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא only means they offer it back and it is refused.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא describes the time before the decree, when robbers really paid back.

steps.title: Using רב נחמן's rule, both sources can be from after the decree
steps.stepSummary: Because רב נחמן limited the תקנה to cases where the stolen item is gone, the גמרא says both ברייתות can be from after the תקנה, and there is still no contradiction.
steps.simpleTranslation: And now that רב נחמן said the decree applies only when the stolen item no longer exists, you can even say that both sources are from after the decree, and it is not a problem.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a new way to fit the two sources together, and it says both can be from after the תקנה. This line sets up the next move, where the גמרא will explain exactly how they differ.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 26 the answer was based on time: one source is from before the תקנה and one is from after. Now רב נחמן's rule gives a different tool: the תקנה only applies when the stolen thing is gone. So the two sources can differ by case, not by time, and both can still be from after the תקנה.

keyTerms.meaning: And now that [so-and-so] said: we can use his rule to answer differently
The stolen item still exists in its original form
This one and that one, meaning both sources
The rabbinic decree that robbers who repent should not be pushed to pay back
And it is not a problem: the contradiction is about to be solved

steps.confusionAlert: This does not take back the idea that the תקנה exists. It only narrows when the תקנה applies, so that both sources can be from after it.

phrases.english: And now that Rav Nachman has said:
[the decree applies only] where the stolen item no longer exists
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets aren't in the Aramaic, but the גמרא takes them for granted.

phrases.english: you can even say that this one and that one
phrases.notes: "This one and that one" means the two ברייתות that seemed to contradict each other.

phrases.english: are from after the decree;
and it is not difficult,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second resolution to the contradiction that Step 26 solved by dating the sources. This one uses רב נחמן's limit on the תקנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: the difference is whether the stolen item still exists, not whether the source is from before or after the תקנה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We had to say one source was from before the תקנה to explain why money actually leaves the robber's hands.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both sources can be from after the תקנה. The difference between them will depend on whether the stolen item still exists, which the next line will spell out.
